title: Buffer Solutions and Titrations - Chemistry - Indicators and End Point Determination
subject: Chemistry

questions.explain: Indicators are typically weak organic acids ($$ \text{HIn} $$) or bases whose undissociated form ($$ \text{HIn} $$) has a different color than its conjugate ion form ($$ \text{In}^- $$). The color change depends on the pH of the solution.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which criterion is most important when selecting an indicator for a titration?
options: The indicator must be the same color as the acid.
The indicator's pH range for color change must coincide with the steep part of the titration curve (equivalence point).
The indicator must have a $$ \text{p}K_a $$ of exactly 7.0.
The indicator must be phenolphthalein for all titrations.
questions.explain: For an accurate titration, the indicator must change color (its transition range) within the steep vertical section of the pH curve that encompasses the equivalence point. This ensures the end point (color change) matches the equivalence point (stoichiometry).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating a **weak acid** ($$ \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} $$) with a **strong base** ($$ \text{NaOH} $$)?
questions.explain: The equivalence point for a Weak Acid/Strong Base titration occurs at a pH > 7 (typically around 8-9). Phenolphthalein changes color in the basic range (8.3 - 10.0), matching the vertical section of this specific titration curve. Methyl orange would change color far too early.
